set.approach: Start at the Cold Springs trailhead (about 5,600 ft) at the end of FR 8040 and walk the South Climb Trail up the old roadbed to its junction with the Round the Mountain Trail near 6,200 ft. Turn right (northwest) onto the Round the Mountain Trail and follow its up-and-down traverse for roughly two miles, much of it under snow in early season, to the stream draining the Avalanche Glacier basin near 6,100 ft. Follow the stream and the moraines above it to the moraine-filled bowl at about 7,200 ft, where the Avalanche Glacier route and the Southwest Chutes meet. The glacier begins above this bowl, and a camp here shortens the summit day.
set.descent_text: Climb out onto the summit plateau and head for the true summit, then descend the South Spur: cross the crater rim past Pikers Peak and follow the broad snow slopes of Crescent Ridge down to the Lunch Counter flats, where glissading is common on soft snow. From there the South Climb Trail runs down the old roadbed to Cold Springs, so no shuttle is needed if you started there. Going back down the White Salmon and Avalanche Glaciers is possible in good snow but means a short, steep 45-degree entry below the summit saddle and crevasses that open on the northern and western parts of the glacier by midsummer. Carry an axe and rope team for either descent.

review.notes: Ski reports from Cold Springs describe the Round the Mountain traverse to the Avalanche basin (waterfall near 6,100 ft, bowl at 7,200 ft) and the White Salmon entry/crevasses. The South Spur walk-off is the usual way down and matches the stored sibling descents; no source states this exact row's descent. Row has no stored top-out, so descent is kept to the standard South Spur.

set.approach: Start at the Killen Creek trailhead on FR 2329 north of Takhlakh Lake and follow Killen Creek Trail 113 south for about 3.2 miles through lodgepole forest and meadows to the Pacific Crest Trail junction near 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail, a rocky boot path that climbs a volcanic spur for about a mile to High Camp on a flat bench near 6,900 ft; the whole carry is roughly four miles and 2,300 ft. Camp here, since water comes only from snowmelt and the site is very exposed to wind. Above camp the trail ends and the way crosses moraines and old lava flows toward the north side of the mountain, so carry navigation for whiteouts. A Cascade Volcano Pass is required above 7,000 ft.
set.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge, also called the North Cleaver, back toward High Camp. This is a walk-off over loose volcanic scree and boulders and is longer than it looks from above, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below, so spread out and move quickly through the worst sections. A rock band on the ridge can be downclimbed, and a short rope-assisted step is sometimes used by parties uneasy with the exposure. From High Camp retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail 113 to the trailhead.

review.notes: WTA supports trail numbers, distances, High Camp elevation and permit. North Cleaver as the walk-off follows the stored sibling North Ridge/Adams Glacier descents and the existing text (descend via the standard North Ridge); the face's own base location is not sourced so the approach ends at High Camp.

set.descent_text: Reverse the route: from the summit plateau go back down the Boulder Glacier past the crevasses on the upper glacier, whose bridges soften in the afternoon, and down the cleaver to the high camp on Boulder Ridge (about 5,700 ft, or a flat spot near 7,500 ft under the cleaver). Near the base of the ridge a short steep step, often protected with a fixed line, is downclimbed or rappelled. From camp, follow the steep unmaintained boot path down the heather and the rock band to the Boulder Ridge Trail and out to the trailhead; allow roughly 4 to 5 hours from camp to the car. Descending toward Schriebers Meadow instead ends at a different trailhead on the south side and needs a vehicle waiting there.

review.notes: Ski report supports crevasses on the upper glacier, the cleaver, the camp and the short rappel/fixed-rope step near the ridge; route page snippet says the descent retraces the ascent. Schriebers Meadow option kept from the existing text. Mountaineers page was blocked to scripted fetch and read only through search summary.

set.approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (about 3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) and follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing several creeks that run higher in the afternoon than the morning. At about two miles and 4,700 ft you pass the former Kulshan Cabin site, then a signed junction: the left fork goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook and the right fork is the climbers' trail. Take the climbers' trail steeply up the Hogsback moraine ridge to the edge of the Coleman Glacier near 6,000 ft, where most parties camp. In winter and spring the road may be gated miles short of the trailhead, which adds distance, and the glacier is skinned from there toward the Deming.
set.descent_text: Ski or walk off by the way you came up. From the summit plateau drop down the Roman Wall, a snow slope of 35 to 45 degrees that is usually downclimbed or skied with care when it is icy, onto the Deming Glacier. Cross the saddle and ski the Coleman Glacier's upper slopes, picking a line through its crevasses and icefall; snow bridges sag in afternoon sun, and late season can force an end-run to climbers' left. Aim for the Hogsback and the climbers' trail junction near 4,700 ft, then follow Trail 677 out. Cloud can close in fast, so follow your up-track.

review.notes: WTA supports trail, Kulshan Cabin site, junction and creek crossings; ski reports support skiing Deming then Coleman back to Heliotrope following the up-track. Roman Wall angle and crevasse notes follow stored sibling Coleman-Deming. Name has no stored line so the standard Coleman-Deming is assumed.

set.approach: Start at the Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft) at the end of the spur off FS 24, which needs a Northwest Forest Pass. Trail 812 climbs at once, with stacked switchbacks for the first 0.3 mile before it merges with the lower-trailhead trail near 3,900 ft. Continue up through forest to the signed junction near timberline, about 4,500 ft, where the winter climbers' route leaves the summer trail and goes right. Follow the heavily used footpath along the north fork of Big Creek into the basin below the south-face chute, which is the base of the climb and a usual place for a first break.
set.descent_text: Descend the chute you climbed. When the snow is continuous, most parties glissade it with an axe in hand, losing roughly 1,000 ft quickly; only do so in control, because a fall on firm or icy snow, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower down, can injure. If the snow is hard near the top, face in and use crampons for the first part, and in a thaw the surface turns sloppy and post-holes. At the foot of the chute, rejoin the climbers' path through the basin to the timberline junction and follow Trail 812 down to the Upper Trailhead. Late in the season, when the snow runs out, use the summer trail.

review.notes: WTA supports trailhead, elevations, 0.3-mile switchbacks, merge at 3,900 ft and winter-route junction; trip report supports the basin below the south-face chute and the descent conditions. Assumes Southeast Chute is the same winter/spring chute (matches stored sibling Standard Trail).

set.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, hug the tree line left, following cairns up heather to the outlet of the lower La Bohn Lake, then continue to the upper lake; the ridge above it is the start of the climb.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ridge to La Bohn Lakes. The rock on the ridge is loose, with blocks that shift underfoot, so test holds and keep clear of other parties. From the lakes, drop back to Necklace Valley either by the heather and cairn line along the tree line or by the boulder gully and stream below La Bohn Gap, which is mostly class 2; in early season the snow chute to the gap needs an ice axe and often crampons. Then follow Necklace Valley trail down past the lakes, the steep 2,400 ft switchbacks and the footlog, and out the flat five miles to the trailhead.

review.notes: WTA trail page supports mileage and gain to Jade Lake and the La Bohn access; trip reports support the heather route to the lakes, the west ridge, loose rock and the gap descent options. Glacier remnant omitted because reports say it is largely gone.

set.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, climb the boulder gully or the waterfall route to La Bohn Gap (about 6,000 ft); the snow chute is the early-season option and needs an axe. The route starts from the gap, where a clear climbers' boot track turns north.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ridge and boot track to La Bohn Gap, downclimbing the class 2 to 3 rock, which is loose throughout. From the gap descend to the valley floor by the boulder gully, by the waterfall route beside it, or by the snow chute when it is soft; hard early-season snow calls for an axe and crampons. Then follow Necklace Valley trail past the lakes, down the steep 2,400 ft switchbacks to the footlog across the East Fork Foss River, and out the five gentle miles to the trailhead.

review.notes: Reports support the La Bohn Gap options (boulder gully, waterfall route, snow chute). The boot track north from the gap onto the southeast ridge was seen only in a search summary of a blocked SummitPost page.
